name: No Breakfast Plan

lead: The No-Breakfast Plan comes from American physician Edward Hooker Dewey, who argued in the 1890s and 1900s that people eat too often and that omitting breakfast lets the body 'rest' and clear itself. Followers framed it as a detox-style routine for staying lean, energetic and healthy-looking.

The route to better looks is the one proponents describe: fewer meals and a daily fasting window mean lower food intake, which can mean less body fat. Modern intermittent-fasting and breakfast-skipping research is a separate body of work, and the 2021 trial that appears in the literature on skipping breakfast examined a rice-based breakfast in adolescents rather than Dewey's plan itself.

paras: In its original form the plan is simple: eat two meals a day, with the first in the late morning or midday, and take no breakfast. Dewey also wrote about longer fasts during illness. Modern readers tend to compare it with time-restricted eating, where the eating window is shortened and the morning meal is dropped.

Medical commentators of Dewey's own era criticised his claims that fasting cures disease. His follower Linda Hazzard ran a Washington State sanatorium where several patients died during prolonged fasts, and she was imprisoned. Skipping breakfast on its own is a mild change, but prolonged fasting carries well-documented medical risks, and people who are growing, pregnant, diabetic or underweight are generally advised by clinicians to seek medical guidance.

angle.text: Followers present the two-meal pattern as a simple way to cut intake and 'rest' digestion, which they associate with a leaner frame and fresher skin. Dewey himself framed the benefits in terms of general health.

lead: The No-Breakfast Plan is a dietary doctrine developed by the American physician Edward Hooker Dewey (1837-1904) and published most fully in his 1900 book The No-Breakfast Plan and the Fasting-Cure [1]. Its central rule is to eat two meals a day and omit breakfast, on the theory that excess eating is the root of much illness and that the digestive system needs rest [1].

For people interested in appearance, the plan fits a familiar chain: a skipped meal and a longer fasting window reduce food intake, which proponents associate with leanness, clearer skin and more energy. Dewey's own writing presented the plan as a route to health without drugs rather than as cosmetic advice, and its modern echo is the 'detox' and intermittent-fasting culture.

Dewey's ideas were popular in the Progressive Era and had a following that included alternative-health writers, but the British Medical Journal in 1910 criticised his accuracy and rejected the idea that fasting cures disease [1]. His student Linda Hazzard became notorious after patients died at her fasting sanatorium [1].

paras: Dewey was born in Wayland, Pennsylvania in 1837, trained at the University of Michigan medical school (graduating 1864), served as an Army assistant surgeon and practised in Meadville, Pennsylvania from 1866 [1]. His books include The True Science of Living (1895), A New Era for Women: Health Without Drugs (1896), Chronic Alcoholism (1899) and The No-Breakfast Plan and the Fasting-Cure (1900), the last of which was his most successful, reached three editions by 1921 and was translated into French and German [1].
He influenced alternative-health writers including Hereward Carrington and Wallace Wattles, and Linda Hazzard studied under him before writing her own book on fasting [1].

Dewey held that people should skip breakfast and eat two meals, that overeating underlay almost all disease, that long fasts were beneficial and that abstaining from food could help even mental disorders. He also argued the plan was consistent with Christian teaching [1].

The British Medical Journal in 1910 described Dewey as an inaccurate and careless writer and dismissed the idea that fasting cures disease. Physician William Tibbles in 1914 accepted that moderate fasting can help under medical supervision but argued Dewey took the practice to an irrational extreme [1].
Contemporary research on breakfast concerns different questions from Dewey's. For example, a randomized trial in Korean adolescents who habitually skip breakfast tested a rice-based breakfast [2].
Hazzard promoted fasting as a treatment and ran a sanatorium in Washington State in the early 1900s where several patients died; she was later imprisoned [1].

No studies of Dewey's No-Breakfast Plan itself have been published. A related 2021 randomized, parallel-group trial enrolled 105 Korean middle and high school students aged 12-18 who habitually skipped breakfast and examined the effects of a rice-based breakfast [2].
